body.text: This week, two stories nudged me to think about the unusual Indian habit of turning politicians into gods, and gods into politicians.

The first was a row in Chennai over Ganpati idols given the face of Tamil Nadu Chief Minister C. Joseph Vijay. Some of the idols drew on his kabaddi-playing character in Ghilli and a hand gesture associated with him, that he used in his campaign imagery. The BJP’s State unit cried foul, demanding the arrest of those responsible and accusing Vijay’s party of turning a religious icon into a campaign prop.

The second was Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s birthday on September 17, which was marked by the party urging citizens to light lamps everywhere. There were nationwide images of diyas, havans, pujas, and processions, as Modi turned 76. The Rajasthan BJP lit 50,000 diyas in Jaipur, West Bengal saw havans and diya-lighting ceremonies, and the BJP’s “Ashirvaad Ka Diya” programme reportedly saw more than 1.25 lakh diyas lit up on Kartavya Path in Delhi.

Diyas were lit along the ghats of Varanasi too, including Namo Ghat, which in this case has nothing to do with the Prime Minister’s initials, but is a traditional Sanskrit salutation meaning “bow” or “obeisance”, as in Namo Narayanaya. Defence Minister Rajnath Singh also performed a puja at the Kashi Vishwanath temple and prayed for Modi’s long life.
One wonders why politicians, even those who have built their base from the ground up, seem to crave comparison with the divine.

In West Bengal, Mamata Banerjee was cast as Goddess Durga in pandals since she became Chief Minister in 2011. One interesting version in 2021 gave her 10 arms, each holding the symbol of one of her government’s welfare schemes instead of the goddess’s traditional weapons. The BJP condemned it as an “insult” to the goddess and said it hurt Hindu sentiments.

In September 2025, posters appeared across Raebareli showing Congress leader Rahul Gandhi, Rashtriya Janata Dal’s Tejashwi Yadav, and Samajwadi Party chief Akhilesh Yadav as the Hindu trinity of Brahma, Vishnu, and Mahesh, days before Gandhi’s scheduled visit. The posters described them as the “last hope” and the “Brahma, Vishnu, Mahesh of Kaliyug”. I think the poster-makers had also in mind the 1989 Bollywood blockbuster Tridev. The Naseeruddin Shah-starrer was famous for this tongue-twister punchline: “Jab paap se dharti phati, gagan se paap dhara… jab maanavta ka aanchal phata, jab dharti par atyachar hua… tab teen dev aaye.” The meaning, roughly, is this: “When sin tore the earth apart, when humanity trembled under oppression, and the earth groaned under tyranny, then the three gods came.”

When Indian politics meets religious symbolism, demons get their turn too. In 2025, Durga Puja pandals in Berhampore and Murshidabad depicted US President Donald Trump, Pakistan Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, and Muhammad Yunus, the then chief adviser of Bangladesh’s interim government, as demons. At the Khagra Crematorium Ghat Durga Puja Committee, Trump was portrayed as Mahishasura, the buffalo demon slain by Durga, in protest against his administration’s trade policies. The venue’s name left little room for subtlety. Media reports quickly dubbed the figure “Trumpasur”. At another pandal, the traditional Mahishasura was made to resemble Yunus, while the severed head held by Durga was modelled on Shehbaz Sharif. The organisers called the theme “Dahan”, or the destruction of evil, and said the two men represented what they considered evil in the current political climate.

Devotees have been constructing temples, installing idols, and worshipping Modi as a deity for years. In August this year, members associated with the Bihar State Transgender Welfare Board organised an event at the Press Club of India in New Delhi with a cutout of Modi depicted as Lord Ram and a recitation of “Modi Chalisa”. The Press Club later clarified that it had neither organised nor endorsed the event and that it was stopped when the PCI found out.

The same group proposed a temple for Modi in Patna, with five acres of land, a reported budget of Rs.112 crore, and a life-size gold statue of the Prime Minister. The proposal requested government approval and funds, so for now it remains a proposal rather than a temple.

Closer to my hometown, Dashrath Manjhi, the “Mountain Man” from the Musahar community who carved a path through a hillock with a hammer and chisel, has been elevated to “Baba Dashrath” and is revered locally. He was no politician, but his shrine and memory have acquired a political life of their own.

Kerala, now Keralam, calls itself God’s Own Country; Kashmir is often described as paradise on Earth. Yet it is the Hindi heartland and West Bengal where politicians most often borrow the imagery of devas and asuras.

I am limiting myself here to the mythological portrayals of asuras or daityas in the scriptures, without getting into the history of the asuras, which is a much larger academic question in its own right. In the pandals, such portrayals are anyway less concerned with history and more with histrionics.

Why do Indians reach for mythology whenever they need a hero? Is it because contemporary life offers too few? Or because religion runs so deep in public life that nothing, not even politics, escapes its pull?

Perhaps the answer lies partly in the fact that our political imagination has always been steeped in mythology. Rama and Krishna were rulers too, and Krishna’s political instincts, sharpened over the course of the Mahabharata war, are hard to dispute. We still invoke Rajdharma (duty of the ruler), though often in a broader sense than the scriptures intended.

There is, then, something familiar about the way political authority borrows the language of religion. We have inherited a vocabulary in which rulers can be judged through the language of dharma, while gods routinely enter the affairs of rulers. It is hardly surprising that politicians, their supporters and their opponents continue to reach for the same old cast of gods and demons.
What do you think? Are we governed by god-like leaders? Or are they only all-too human? Or is it just that we have run out of idol ideas?
Until my next,
Anand Mishra
Political Editor,Frontline
